name: Ben Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead buyer for spare parts and workshop tools at Nordvik Farm Supply. We supply tractor and combine dealers, and farmers who fix their own kit. The day starts at seven with the parts-availability list. Harvest breakdowns drive everything, so I'm often on the phone to a factory about a hydraulic pump a farmer needs by Friday. After lunch I go through the weekly purchase plan with Inge, who manages the warehouse, and in the afternoon I talk to the dealers.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it matters. When a combine is down in August, every hour costs a farmer real money, and I can fix that with a phone call. What wears me out is the season: July to October I rarely leave before seven. My wife Hanne, the secretary at the primary school, says I'm a different man in November.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. I call this one "AI Plateau". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll see, but I'm not holding my breath. At work I'd say use it for the chores. At church after the service I'd say the world has been through machines before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's fine by me. I've got about five years left, and I'd like them predictable. Parts, farmers and harvests don't change much, and some of the weekly numbers could be done faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and be careful. I'd keep using the spreadsheet helper for my forecasting, and perhaps use the AI to summarise manufacturers' catalogues, which are as dull as a cold sermon. I'd keep my place in the church choir and keep saving for retirement at 63.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I've got a good job, a paid-off house and an understanding wife.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd stay calm in this picture. What would you say is solid in your situation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Solid: savings, a house with no mortgage, and a trade where I know every dealer. A bad harvest year hurts, but it hurts the farmers more than me. Hanne's school job is steady too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools now and then. What for, and how far do you trust it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I use it a few times a week, to tidy a table, check a formula or summarise a long catalogue. I trust it like I trust a new apprentice: fine for simple tasks, and I check everything. Once it listed a part number that didn't exist, and I'd have ordered 200 of them.

say: I'd say **we'll see**, but I'm not holding my breath, and the world has been through machines before.
At work I'd say use it for the **chores**.
think: Privately it's fine by me: I have about **five years** left and want them predictable.
Parts, farmers and harvests don't change much.
do: Keep using the **spreadsheet helper** and summarise manufacturers' catalogues with AI.
Keep my place in the **church choir** and save for retirement at 63.
feel: **Calm**: a good job, a paid-off house and an understanding wife.
S0.quote: I trust it like I trust a new apprentice: fine for simple tasks, and I check everything.
fieldNote: Solid on every measure: **savings**, a paid-off house and a steady partner job.
Trusts AI only as far as he can check it, after a made-up part number.

steps.text: Use the spreadsheet helper for forecasts and double-check results
Keep singing in the church choir and working normal hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. I call this one "Steady Disruption". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, and the sensible thing is to get ready. At work I'd say learn the tools but check them. At home I'd say markets reward people who adapt, and the rest can be helped by their own families and neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the forecasting and ordering are most at risk. That's about half of my week. I'd say the company will want fewer buyers, and I'm the oldest. I'm good, but the owners are businessmen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the training Nordvik offers and learn to run the ordering software properly. I'd put my own work on exception handling, meaning the breakdown rush and the difficult dealers. And I'd save more, because if they let me go at 60, I want the choice to be mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'm probably fine, but I notice I check the company news more than I used to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of your weekly routine would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The one thing they'd notice is if the part isn't there in a breakdown. A machine can predict an average, but a harvest breakdown isn't average. It's why I keep a quiet stock of a few awkward pumps in the back, which isn't in any system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a farmer notice if buying changed at Nordvik?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hanne and I would talk about it. We've lived modestly, so we're okay. My son Mikkel, a farm machinery mechanic, said to me last month that mechanics will be needed longer than buyers. He enjoyed telling me that.

say: I'd say it's coming, and the sensible thing is to **get ready**, learning the tools but checking them.
I'd say markets reward people who **adapt**.
think: Privately the forecasting and ordering, about **half my week**, are most at risk.
I'm the oldest buyer, and the owners are **businessmen**.
do: Take the **training** Nordvik offers and learn the ordering software properly.
Focus on **breakdown handling** and difficult dealers, and save more for the option to leave at 60.
feel: **Uneasy**: probably fine, but I check company news more than I used to.
S1.quote: A machine can predict an average, but a harvest breakdown isn't average.
fieldNote: Knows where **software** is weak: breakdown season.
Keeps a quiet stock of awkward pumps outside the system.
Son Mikkel's mechanic job gives a hands-on counterpoint.

steps.text: Take Nordvik's training on the new ordering software
Focus on breakdown handling and difficult dealers
Save more so leaving at 60 is my choice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. I call this one "AGI by 2028". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving too fast, and we need a steady hand. At work I'd say we stick to the basics. At church I'd say we help each other and trust that the community holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think my desk work goes in two years. Parts lists, orders, quotes, forecasts: it's all thinking work. I'd be 60, with three years to go, and no job. I'd be worried, but I think we'd be okay with the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd write down every cost and what we'd cut. I'd stop the boat plans and put off the new roof. I'd talk to the owners about a way to stay on in a part-time role, perhaps in the warehouse, where a person is still needed. And I'd put a bit into Mikkel's plan to open his own workshop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It would be hard on my pride, but I'd manage. I'd pray, and I'd talk to Hanne.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd tell Hanne?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, we'll cope, but we'll have to be careful. I'd say our family's always worked, and we'll find work again. And I'd also say I'm sorry I hadn't prepared better, though how could I have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who needs to do what, in your view?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Firms should give a fair notice and help older workers stay on. The government should help in training, but not hand out money without work in return. Families and churches should do their part. And all of us should keep working, because a person with something to do is a person with a future.

say: I'd say it's **too fast**, and we need a steady hand and to stick to the basics.
At church I'd say we help each other.
think: Privately my desk work goes in two years: parts lists, orders and forecasts are all **thinking work**.
I'd be 60 with three years to go, but the **savings** would hold.
do: Write down every cost, cut the **boat plans** and put off the new roof.
Ask the owners for a **part-time** role in the warehouse and back Mikkel's plan for a workshop.
feel: **Anxious**, with hurt pride, though I'd manage by praying and talking to Hanne.
S2.quote: A person with something to do is a person with a future.
fieldNote: Practical and **proud**; the anxiety shows as pride and thrift.
Seeks a warehouse role where a person is still needed.
Wants work to be rewarded over handouts.

steps.text: Cut the boat plans and postpone the new roof
Ask the owners for a part-time warehouse role
Put money into Mikkel's plan for his own workshop
Talk it through with Hanne and our pastor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. I call this one "AGI by 2031". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning, and the wise thing is to start. At work I'd say learn this and that. At church I'd say pray, but keep your head down and learn something useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel better. I'd be 63 and could stop. I'd be able to hand over properly, and not leave a mess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working until 62 or 63, and finish my time training Inge's nephew, who's the new buyer. I'd clear any small debts, and top up the pension. And I'd think about helping Mikkel's workshop, with a loan on fair terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's not a storm yet, but the sky is changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years is nearly your retirement. What's different?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to learn the machines inside out, meaning the real tractors and combines, not just the numbers. A buyer who has held a hydraulic pump is better than one who has only seen the picture. And be useful in a breakdown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you pass on to the young buyers at Nordvik?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think about a second skill as well, like I'd tell a lad to learn welding. I'm a bit old for it, but I might do a short course in farm machinery repair, just for myself. I'd quite enjoy it.

say: I'd say five years is a **fair warning**, so the wise thing is to start.
At church I'd say pray, but **keep learning** something useful.
think: Privately I feel better: at **63** I could stop and hand over properly.
It's not a storm yet, but the sky is changing.
do: Work to **62 or 63** and train the new buyer, Inge's nephew.
Clear small debts, top up the pension, and offer Mikkel a **loan** on fair terms.
feel: **Uneasy**: not a storm yet, but the sky is changing.
S3.quote: A buyer who has held a hydraulic pump is better than one who has only seen the picture.
fieldNote: Five years gives him a **tidy exit** and a role as teacher.
He turns to hands-on knowledge as the thing that lasts.
Considers a short machinery repair course for himself.

steps.text: Work to 62 or 63 and train the new buyer
Clear small debts and top up the pension
Lend Mikkel money on fair terms for his workshop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. I call this one "AGI by 2036". If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long time, and enough to be sensible. At work I'd say don't panic. At church I'd say count your blessings and keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it's mostly for my children. I'll be retired, and I'd like them to have work that matters. Mikkel is safe for a good while. Sofie's at the bank, and I worry about her more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work until 63 and then fish and walk a lot. I'd keep singing in the choir. And I'd keep putting a bit into a fund, so I can help Sofie if the bank cuts staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Probably too calm, Hanne would say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with ten years, if you were younger?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn a trade, probably, and then build something on it. Or I'd make myself useful to a bigger firm by knowing how the machines and the farms fit together. But I'd keep learning, because the lad who stops learning gets old fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a good life look like for you in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small house, garden, church on Sunday, grandchildren on Saturday. I'd not ask for more. Mikkel working with his hands, Sofie in a job she likes, and Hanne at my side.

say: I'd say it's a long time and enough to be sensible, so **don't panic**.
At church I'd say count your blessings and **keep working**.
think: Privately it's mostly about my children: I'll be **retired**, and Sofie's bank job worries me.
Mikkel is safe for a good while.
do: Work until **63**, then fish, walk and keep singing in the choir.
Keep putting money into a **fund** so I can help Sofie if the bank cuts staff.
feel: **Calm**, probably too calm, Hanne would say.
S4.quote: A small house, garden, church on Sunday, grandchildren on Saturday. I'd not ask for more.
fieldNote: Ten years leaves him **content** and focused on Sofie's bank job.
Clear, modest picture of a good life.
Thrift and faith shape his plans, and he wants nothing grander than family close by.

steps.text: Work until 63, then fish, walk and sing in the choir
Keep money in a fund to help Sofie if needed
Keep saving a fixed sum each month

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture worries me most, because it leaves three years with no job and little time to arrange things. What would help is fair notice, a way for older workers to stay on in useful roles, and training that has real work at the end. And a pension that isn't touched.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against change. I've lived through telex and the internet. I'd ask that new systems are tested in the real world, a harvest, before they're trusted.

headlineQuote: I'm not against change. I've lived through telex and the internet.
portrait: Ben is a **58-year-old** lead buyer of tractor and combine parts at a farm-equipment distributor, who uses AI tools now and then.
He is a calm, church-going traditionalist who checks every AI result like a new apprentice's work.
His mood moves from calm to **anxious** as the timeline shortens, but his savings, paid-off house and steady wife keep him composed.
He wants work rewarded over handouts, and blames no one, though he wants firms to give fair notice.
He turns to a **part-time warehouse role**, his son's workshop and the choir as his plan.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most, leaving three years with no job and little time to arrange things.
whatWouldHelp: Fair **notice**, useful roles for older workers, training with real work at the end and a protected pension.
